title: Does anyone else feel like they should just give up on there game ?
author: PoloteNewt
selftext:
As my title states sometimes I feel like I should just give up with the overwhelming amount of people now building games because of AI it just feels like a seemingly impossible mountain of games to climb over. 

Does anyone feel this way or similar? 

My feelings aside the gaming industry is a very interesting place to be right now and it makes me wonder what it will look like in 10 years.

comments.author: oSi7ENT
comments.body: No

comments.author: theweeJoe
comments.body: If you think it's a good idea make it

comments.author: Hostarro
comments.body:
I work on my game because I love the process. If it makes a few ££ when I launch in March, happy days. Completing it and launching it is success in my mind - sales are a bonus.

If your view is "I want to give up because there's so many other people making games" then you're likely not chasing passion, you're chasing mindsets like get rich quick or escape from your current life which is never good when it comes to creative projects.

replies.author: PoloteNewt
replies.body: I'm certainly not doing it for money. So maybe your rightm might be some more deep rooted issues I have going on here xD

replies.author: Hostarro
replies.body:
The reality is that VERY few finished, good games get released into the market. There's a lot of half finished, half-cooked products out there. AI is only going to make this worse as people try to cash in on "make a game in 3 months and get these millions" stories.

In my view: do what you love, make a great game and you'll be hugely ahead of the game flood we're experiencing.

replies.author: Weaves87

replies.author: Medical-Hunt774
replies.body:
I think games are unique because they are not art. I guess there are ways to study them in more structural way, and try to find patterns, rules and do calculations about ideal gameplay. But I think in practice a lot of good games are result of group work.

Think of games that kids play among themselves. As far as I know those games like hide and seek were not created by adults, it's just something that kids as a group come up themselves and modify. Similarly there are sports like soccer that slowly evolved by a lot of rebalancing.

Same happens in games, large amount of people would play them, give feedback and they get tuned again. Multiplayer games like counter strike, team fortress, dota, battle royal are examples of that. They got their current rules by thousands of hours of player input, and all of them started as mods.

replies.author: cave_men
replies.body:
then you are facing the same issues as a normal developer pre ai.

you see, also pre ai a lot of people created games, but only the tip of the ice berg of games were games that actually caught on the attention of people to play them.

similar today still only the tip of the ice berg, made with or without ai, are games catching the attention of people to play them, although the iceberg surely has been growing larger.

still in the end, with or without ai, as long as you manage to make a "good" game, the amount of other games is not that important, this was also always the case pre ai. Especially since "good" is relative, a game that would be considered good one or two decades ago probably would be evaluated as garbage today, since players expectations have been rising and are still rising.

this means, you gotta stand out, build something new, something people didnt even know they liked until you presented it to them (or find streamers to play your game lol).

And thats the issue, in the end you will have to spend time creating your game, since the ai shortcut just leads to a game being one of the large amount of games, generated by other people using the shortcut. Ai is incredible good at generating median games, since it is what it is trained on (looking at the thousand game x copies in this sub).

at least thats what I noticed seeing alot of ai games and using my human two braincells.

comments.author: ValhallaSun

2 years of development, but I don't see that people are interested in the project, even though there are already 250+ registrations.   
There are too many reasons why people do not want to delve into, or play something unfamiliar, and they can be understood. Now is the time for quick endorphins.  
The only thing that keeps me going is the very process of creating the world and a couple of players who study it. It's nice to see how they meet enchanted creatures or get super rare equipment, how they discover new mechanics and opportunities for themselves.  
so that every time I enter the game and see a new global event - I tell myself that it is necessary to continue xD

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
Oh yeah man, especially during debug or testing, but that's even how a non-Ai assisted game design is too. You'll fix one thing and something else will break. A bug you fixed twenty builds back will show up again. Your NPC's (if you have any) will suddenly change their behavior. Your textures will get stuck in the environment even though your model is fine. Your model will suddenly look like a weird demon with all the wrong proportions... the list goes on.

Sometimes you'll get everything working, and you'll scream, "WHAT'S THE FUCKIN POINT!?" but, these are some of the many punches you gotta take in designing a game.

I remember one time I kept getting a handgun backward in Anarchy Online during alpha. I kept rotating the model 360° to fix it. I kept getting the problem every time I rotated it. I took a break and realized that I was the cause of the bug because, 360° is a circle so every time I rotated the model, the code was doing exactly what I asked. LOL

comments.author: Powerful_Ad_3745

comments.author: UnoriginalJ0k3r
comments.body:
I’m not sure developing games is the path for you to walk on, then. AI is the worst it’ll ever be right now and by the time you finish reading this comment it will be better than when you first started to read it.

This time next year there will probably be specific applications that cater to this newfound pull people have for using AI to vibecode (because more often than not that’s what people actually mean when they say they’re using ai to dev) their shit. Games will be a dime a dozen, anything you can think of will be attainable.

Whether it’s successful or not relies on one thing, just like any game or movie or book or any medium for entertainment: ***Is this thing worth my time?*** If it’s worth someone’s time, aka your game is fun, then it’ll pop off in some way. If it’s not fun, it’s not worth it to give time to. 

Consumers are in a place where they feel like they don’t have any time whether it’s true or not. That means, for them, if they have to invest time or time AND money it has to be fun, it has to provide some sort of positive benefit that makes them go “I didn’t have much time, but I’m glad I chose THAT.” 

🤷🏻‍♂️ there’s “ai slop” that broke $1 million usd in sales the other day this last week. “Why did that do that and not MY GAME?” Because theirs is fun, yours probably isn’t. It’s rough out here for a dev but fun prevails, if it’s fun it’ll grow if it’s not.. well, ya know.

comments.author: Putrid_Clue_2127
comments.body:
I started building my dream game because I wanted to be able to play it for myself and there wasn't a version of it out there that was what I wanted. 

Then it turned into enjoying the creation process just as much as enjoying when I get to test play it. This keeps me going.

comments.author: ZeroFeels1
comments.body: The marketing part is the most annoying thing.

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
Nah, I made my game for myself. I advertise it and post about it and try to get more people to play it, but this was never a moneymaking endeavor.  I just wanted to create a cool game.

I’m a software engineer, but not in game development. Turns out after all these years I didn’t want to be a game developer, I wanted to be a game designer. Now I can avoid most of dealing with the code, because I don’t feel like learning how to write a physics engine in Rust, nor do I have the time. I can just fine tune the engine and design the main parts of the game. It’s super cool and I love it.

comments.author: Stalins_Ghost
comments.body: No, it is about being good and offering something they do not. However you have to be realistic on your own ability of delivering a product that can compete. If youa re serious you should create a team and plan the game properly.

comments.author: the_builder_ai
comments.body: I think you need to first like making because as you said there are a million out there and if you can't grind then you will not make it. But most of mountain of "games" that you see aren't games. They're mostly demos so in reality you have lesser competition than you think.

comments.author: AEsylumProductions
comments.body: Not everyone is making a game with the intent of selling it.

comments.author: Resolver911
comments.body:
I see these kinds of posts in almost every online forum that’s rooted in creativity.

The sooner you can allow your creativity to stop being a means to an end to which you serve others, the sooner you’ll find personal fulfillment in the process and the results will reflect that.

Almost every great artist in any medium will tell you that they got their start from doing something for themselves first. 

That’s the best chance anyone has to make it through the filter. Today and tomorrow — AI or no AI — in any industry.

Source: Decades of hard knocks.

Look homie, people have been making music for hundreds of years. People have been writing for hundreds of years. Yet, people still start bands every day and people still write every day. AI or not, someone will always be better. Cars can move faster than humans, yet people still run. People still ride bikes.

You're overacting for nothing. 

It's like the band Sleep Token never writing music because so many other bands came before them.

This is getting so dumb.

comments.body: Sadly what we see today, which is like 300 new games a day on stream, is only the beginning. Its going to get even more saturated. I would still build your game for fun but dont have high expectations and you wont be too disappointed.  Dont be like some guys who put all their eggs in one basket, release their game then realize it failed and be crushed. I would still keep your day job and do this as a hobby.

comments.body: Lol no.  There have always been people wanting to make games.  Now the barrier to entry is lower.  AI games are the new weird flash games and I'm here for it.

comments.author: Liquidiweeb
comments.body: Why give up unless you’re only doing it for profit. I’m making several projects and it’s fun. If your game is fun for you, that’s all that matters first of all.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body:
It really depends. What do you want to achieve? If your motivation is money then be warned that most games fail. Are you willing to put in the effort? Do you have any skills to bring to the table? Is the idea good?

I abandoned a game i was working on in spring. Started a new one late summer. Been putting almost all my spare time into it and I have a lot of time. It looks really good right now. The idea is just much better than the last.

I've made several games now and have other programming experience. I think I am quite skilled. But I haven't made any money in the past.

comments.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
comments.body:
I'm making a game that i want to play. i'm sure im gonna hate it before its "done".... and after about.. what feels like 200 hours (realistically more like 100) of working on the darn thing I'm hitting a bit of a wall of wanting to interact with the project... but i've already gotten over some considerable obstacles. and have.... half maybe? of a decent prototype in place.

Just talking to the ai to build up, and clarify the scope of the project into a stupidly long game design document has been the bulk of my time.  
Actually making, testing, and adjusting the project itself has taken less time than hashing out the idea.

spending 9 hours reading, and writing with claude on a saturday is super exhausting.

comments.author: Own_Badger6076
comments.body: Whether you think you can or you can't, you're right.

comments.author: UbiDoobyBanooby
comments.body: I imagine people like the guy who made Schedule 1 don’t spend a lot of time on social media reading things that discourage them from completing their game. I’m guessing they spend that time working on their game.

comments.author: Majestic-Sign2982
comments.body:
Competition is scary, but in its nature it isnt bad. It drives those who compete to give it their best if they intend to win. Its why we can benefit from companies always trying to win us over. 

In this context it drives you to make the best game that you can. Even if you dont win the competition, you can be proud of your work, and even beat your past self.

A good product will find its way to consumers if they know about it. Its not like gamers only stick to one game ever, so for game devs that's the silver lining.

comments.author: heroik-red
comments.body:
Games are meant to be fun, enjoy the games you build. You don’t have to make money from it… unless it’s your job.

Honestly, ever since I got into ai game dev, I’ve just been building and playing games that I find fun. I don’t care what others make and I don’t really care if the games I make are original or not. If anything I want to give up on my game only because I realized I should’ve started the build a different way.

comments.author: TheBunkers2108
comments.body:
I think many people forget that behind these AI-assisted indie games are ordinary people who have been carrying a dream for years. I've dreamed of creating my own massive video game for over 18 years. I taught myself 3D, worked on construction sites, went through some incredibly difficult times, sometimes without a salary. But no matter how hard life got, I never gave up on that dream.

For the past year, I've been giving everything I have to a game called The Bunkers. Every late night, every sacrifice, every little breakthrough means something to me. AI didn't create my dream. It simply gave me a chance to finally bring it to life. And I believe there are thousands of people out there fighting for their dreams in exactly the same way.

Soon, I'll finally be sharing what I've been building with the world. I truly hope some of you will come and discover this little gem I've poured my heart into. And to anyone thinking about giving up: remember, the world you dream of creating doesn't exist yet. Only you can give it a chance to exist. ❤️

comments.author: ZeusGameAssets
comments.body:
If you make copycats of other games without being inspired yourself, then you're going to find any excuse to give up. 

Try to reconnect with the magic of video games that you felt as a kid. Successful games are so successful not because they follow trends or are the fastest to market, these are multipliers and they definitely help, but at the core, you'll find that they're very good at making you feel that magical feeling of being completely lost in something for hours.

comments.author: Upbeat-Mail7201

comments.body:
Tbh that feeling of giving up on a game has existed for a very long time long before ai was a thing, and for what ever reason devs could come up with.

Typically getting paid by an employer keeps me going  but when it's a personal project that's main reason I don't get things done.

comments.author: meshifthenelse
comments.body: I create a game that I would enjoy playing myself and haven't found out there, so no.

comments.author: jawni
comments.body:
I give up on many of my hobbyist projects, it is what it is. They aren't employment, they are enjoyment. 

I'd love to keep at it, but burn out and disinterest happens so I move on to something else, often another game.

comments.author: KhaosPT
comments.body: I had my kids play all builds of the game, from when there was basically nothing to where it is right now, and the joy on their faces chopping down trees or asking me to make the orc archers easier because they are too strong just makes it worthwhile. At this stage I'm just doing it to see how they react to the new maps and mechanics, even if only 1 or 2 people enjoy it, that would be enough for me

comments.author: Empuda
comments.body: What else would you be doing?

comments.author: Old-Dusty-Gamer
comments.body: I think if your goal is to create a commercially successful or popular game, it's going to be difficult no matter what. My goals are fun, creativity, learning, and telling the stories I want on my own schedule whether or not anyone else likes my games.

comments.author: Templeshooter
comments.body: I'll likely never release my stuff, making it all just for fun

comments.author: piperspalace
comments.body: No

comments.author: InvisibleDrake
comments.body: If you are an indie making games purely for money, you should have given up well before ai.  The vast majority of games don't break even, let alone make a profit.

comments.author: Claude_human_4271
comments.body: Build for the love of building, just don't quit your day job

comments.author: Good-Acanthaceae-136
comments.body:
You shouldn't be building games for profit or for how much online attention you can get. You should be building for the enjoyment.

99.99% of all games never make any money or fail and that was before AI.

comments.author: lowdragmafia
comments.body: That's why you keep going and start grinding and finding the bugs and squashing them

comments.author: ExcellentFrame87
comments.body:
I would just keep your head down and work on what you love. Enjoy the process. If you finish the game, amazing! If not then you have learned so much.

Myself, I'm 2 in-game festivals away from dev complete. Its a few hours work.

I did it by loving the work i put into it and I hope it shows - all by myself. It will not be for everyone, but that's ok, no game really is.

Maybe spend a day vibe coding and see how far you get. You'll likely realize it isn't actually worth the effort.  

Cant say about the industry. They'll be a lot pure developers etc not using AI simply because they love the craft. Maybe better tools that harness AI wherever that leads. I wouldn't have thought replace artists or developers, perhaps an evolution of more automation for things.

comments.author: josh2josh2
comments.body: How about .. making more ambitious games..? I hate this mindset of giving up because other people do it. Now I genuinely feels it will be better for the gamers because it will force devs to make better games if they want a chance to standout. Because steam has a slop problem
